en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sahadhammika-vagga 80.
The Training Rule on Going After Having Given One’s Consent.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Saṅgha was assembled for some business or other.
While the group of six monks were engaged in robe-making, they gave their consent (*chanda*) to one [of them].
Then the Saṅgha, thinking, "We shall perform that action for which we have assembled," put forward a motion (*ñatti*).

Then that bhikkhu, thinking, "In this very way they are performing the legal act against each individual; against whom will you perform the legal act? did not give his consent and, rising from his seat, departed.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“How indeed can a bhikkhu, when a formal discussion of a legal matter is underway in the Saṅgha, depart from his seat and leave without having given his consent? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhu, that you departed from your seat and left while a formal discussion of a legal matter was underway in the Saṅgha, without having given your consent?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, when a formal discussion of legal matters is taking place in the Saṅgha, depart from your seat without having given your consent?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“Whosoever, however, a monk, while a formal discussion of a legal question is taking place in the Saṅgha, should rise from his seat and depart without having given his consent, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, however:
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
Regarding "a legal decision in the Saṅgha":
this refers to when a matter has been announced but not yet decided; or when a motion has been proposed; or when the formal proclamation of the transaction has been interrupted.
To "rise from one's seat and depart without having given consent" means: [to do so].
If he goes thinking, “How can this action be invalid and factional so that it does not take effect? there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For one who leaves the reach of the assembly’s handspan, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
once the reach of the handspan has been left, there is an offense entailing confession.
If it is a legitimate legal procedure (*dhammakamma*) and he perceives it as such, yet he departs from his seat without having given his consent, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If it is a legitimate legal procedure but he is uncertain of it, and he departs from his seat without having given his consent, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If it is a legitimate legal procedure but he perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*), and he departs from his seat without having given his consent, there is no offense.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is unsure of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is no offense.
There is no offense if one goes thinking, "There will be quarreling, strife, contention, or dispute in the Saṅgha," or if one goes thinking,
"There will be a schism in the Saṅgha or a fracture in the Saṅgha."
He goes thinking, “They will perform a legal act against one who is not entitled to it, either by an illegal procedure or with an incomplete assembly”;
he goes because he is ill;
or he goes on account of some business for one who is ill.
If he goes because he is oppressed by the urge to defecate or urinate;
or if he goes thinking, "I do not wish to interrupt my work, I will return again";
or if he is insane.
"Of the first offender":
the tenth training rule concerning departing without having given one's consent is finished.
